report:
### Conclusion

The claim that influenza vaccination causes Alzheimer's disease is unsupported by scientific evidence. Medical research and public health organizations classify this claim as a myth, finding that flu shots do not increase the risk of Alzheimer's and may instead be associated with a reduced risk of developing dementia.

### Evidence Overview

* **Absence of Risk:** Peer-reviewed scientific evidence does not support any link between receiving an influenza vaccine and an increased risk of Alzheimer's disease (https://www.alzdiscovery.org/cognitive-vitality/blog/is-there-a-link-between-alzheimers-disease-and-the-flu-shot). Health advocacy organizations explicitly list the idea that vaccines cause or elevate the risk of Alzheimer's as a common misconception (https://www.alz.org/alzheimers-dementia/what-is-alzheimers/myths).
* **Protective Association:** Multiple observational and retrospective cohort studies indicate that regular flu vaccination is associated with a lower incidence of Alzheimer's disease. For instance, large-scale studies on older adults found up to a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk among flu-vaccinated individuals compared to unvaccinated peers (https://neurosciencenews.com/flu-vaccination-alzheimers-20909/; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9484126/).

In summary, current evidence indicates that influenza vaccines do not cause Alzheimer's disease and may provide a protective benefit against cognitive decline.
